paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Scott and Smith counties, Mississippi, was a campaign in the autumn of 1903 in which white residents whipped the occupants of numerous Black cabins, burned their homes and drove them out of the state. It is known only from a brief New Orleans wire dispatch of mid-November that described "race riots of large proportions" and was reprinted in a handful of papers outside the South.

According to the dispatch, dated at New Orleans on November 14, the violence was still "in progress" in the two counties when it was filed. "The white residents," none of them named, whipped the people living in "numerous negro cabins," set fire to their homes and forced them to leave Mississippi. The Black families fled, the report added, and left their crops standing unharvested in the fields.

The coverage gives no names or numbers of victims, no town, no date on which the attacks began and no reason for them. No one is reported killed, and the dispatch describes no organized band, only the white residents of the area.
No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response to the expulsions appears in the coverage.

The Washington Times printed the dispatch on November 15 on page 10 under the headline "DRIVE NEGROES OUT OF MISSISSIPPI TOWNS," with no comment. Over the following week the same text ran in small weeklies in North and South Dakota, Duluth and Chicago, headed "Race War Mississippi.," "Whipped by Whites.," "NEGROES DRIVEN OUT." and "Lash and Exile Negroes." Editors trimmed and redated it freely: the Pioneer Press of Miller, South Dakota, gave a November 17 dateline and dropped the burning and the crops, while the Labor World of Duluth dated it November 16.

Every version used the language of a "race riot" or "race war" for what it described as whites attacking Black households, and none named a victim, quoted anyone or followed up. No Mississippi paper's account and no Black-press report of the episode appear in the coverage.
